analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal student loan servicing contracts so borrowers are compensated when servicers make errors.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2024 with three Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate education committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal student loans are handled by private and nonprofit servicers hired by the Education Department, and those companies are paid to process payments, forgiveness paperwork, and borrower questions. This bill would require the Department to vet a servicer's track record before hiring it, and would write borrower protections into every servicing contract: if a servicer's error puts a borrower into forbearance, no interest accrues and the period still counts toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness; borrowers get refunds and reimbursement of fees caused by servicer errors; erroneous negative marks must be removed from credit reports; records must be kept; and the Department can revoke a contract if a servicer misled it during vetting. It also directs a nonpartisan study of how loan transfers between servicers damage borrowers' credit.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers, especially those harmed by servicer mistakes: people in income-driven repayment or pursuing Public Service Loan Forgiveness whose progress stalls because of a servicer error, borrowers hit with overdraft or overpayment charges caused by those errors, and borrowers whose credit reports carry negative marks they did not cause. Borrowers with limited English proficiency and borrowers with disabilities get guaranteed access to forms and support in multiple languages and accessible formats.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal student loan borrowers harmed by servicer errors

how_it_helps.text: If a servicer identifies an error but has not yet fixed it, the borrower's loans must be placed into forbearance with no interest accruing during that period, and those months count as qualifying payments toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness and income-driven repayment forgiveness.

Servicers must make borrowers whole when their own errors cause financial harm, including refunding overpayments and reimbursing fees such as insufficient-funds charges, and must ensure credit bureaus remove delinquencies caused by the servicer.

The Education Department must evaluate a servicer's past performance, consumer satisfaction, penalties, legal actions taken by states, and its ability to serve at-risk borrowers, underrepresented communities, and borrowers with disabilities before signing a servicing contract.

Servicers must keep borrower account records for at least three years after accounts close or transfer, and the Department must review all existing 'legacy' contracts to see whether they meet the new standards before renewing them.

The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office must study how loan transfers between servicers cause account errors, credit-report damage, and complaint failures, and report recommendations to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: The student loan servicing companies would bear the cost: interest-free forbearance during their own errors, refunds and reimbursements, longer record retention, and the risk of losing a contract for misrepresentation during vetting. The Education Department would take on new vetting, review, and annual reporting duties. Some compliance costs could ultimately flow to taxpayers through servicing contract prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan servicing companies and the Education Department

drawbacks.text: The bill adds significant compliance obligations — no-interest forbearance whenever a servicer spots an error, refunds, reimbursements, and multi-year record retention — and servicing companies could pass those costs back to taxpayers through contract bids, while heavier vetting could deter capable firms from bidding at all.

It applies mainly to contracts signed after enactment and directs only a review of existing legacy contracts; borrowers currently stuck with a poorly performing servicer would not automatically get the new protections unless their contract is changed or revoked.

The bill is largely a reporting and process measure: the required reviews and GAO study would take a year or two, and the bill changes no loan balances, interest rates, or repayment terms for borrowers whose servicers perform adequately.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the protections are concrete and targeted at a documented problem — servicer errors that strand people in the wrong repayment status, block forgiveness credit, and ding their credit. The costs fall mainly on servicing companies that are being paid to avoid exactly these errors, though taxpayers could see some of the compliance cost in contract prices. The bill is narrow: it polices how servicers behave rather than lowering what borrowers owe, and it would only fully help new contracts at first. On balance it is a modest, consumer-side repair bill whose main weakness is scope and its reliance on the Department to enforce it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the bill on June 5, 2024, with Senators Klobuchar, Van Hollen, and Padilla as cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
No further action was taken: the committee never held a markup or vote, the full Senate never considered it, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The student loan servicing companies benefit from the outcome: they keep their Department of Education contracts and current terms, with no added obligations to refund overpayments, repair credit records, or count error periods toward forgiveness. Borrowers who relied on Public Service Loan Forgiveness or income-driven repayment gain nothing from a bill that was never voted on.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Student Loan Servicers Accountability Act of 2024.

for.name: 3 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Klobuchar, Van Hollen, and Padilla)

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup, hearing vote, or floor recommendation on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with the bill never leaving committee no vote was ever taken that could test broader support.

industries.note: The bill leaves the contracted-out servicing system fully intact — servicers remain the permanent middlemen between borrowers and the Department — while adding costly obligations on top: no-interest forbearance during their own errors, refunds and fee reimbursements, credit-report cleanup, three-year record retention, and contract revocation for lying during vetting. Servicers profit from per-borrower servicing fees, so mandatory make-whole remedies and error standards cut into revenue without changing their role.

industries.industry: Education Department contractors and vendors (Unified Servicing and Data Solution, business process vendors)
industries.note: The bill extends the same vetting, contract terms, and revocation authority to data and business-process vendors, not just servicers, and asks a GAO study of whether the new unified servicing data system actually fixes transfer errors — tighter oversight with no change in who holds the work.
